Her face changed colour, and she fell silent.

Mrs. Gardiner stood a little way behind them. When Elizabeth stopped speaking, he politely asked her to introduce him to her friends. She had not expected such courtesy, and could hardly keep from smiling. Here he was, seeking an introduction to some of the very people his pride had objected to when he proposed to her. “How astonished he will be,” she thought, “when he discovers who they are! He supposes they are fashionable people.”

Still, she introduced them immediately. As she explained how they were related to her, she stole a sideways glance at him to see his reaction. She half expected him to hurry away from such embarrassing company. He was clearly surprised to hear of the connection, but he bore the discovery bravely. Instead of leaving, he turned and walked back with them, beginning a conversation with Mr. Gardiner. Elizabeth could not help feeling pleased and triumphant. It comforted her that he should discover she had relatives of whom she need not feel ashamed. She paid close attention to their conversation and took pride in every phrase and remark of her uncle’s that showed his intelligence, taste, or good manners.

Before long they began discussing fishing. She heard Mr. Darcy, with great politeness, invite her uncle to fish there whenever he wished for as long as he stayed nearby. He also offered to lend him fishing equipment and pointed out the stretches of the stream where the fishing was generally best. Mrs. Gardiner, walking with her arm through Elizabeth’s, gave her a look of astonishment. Elizabeth said nothing, but she felt deeply pleased; surely this courtesy was all on her account. Yet she was also utterly bewildered. Again and again she thought, “Why has he changed so much? What can have caused it? Surely he cannot have become so much gentler because of me, for my sake. My criticisms at Hunsford could not have brought about a change like this. He cannot possibly still love me.”

They walked in this arrangement for some time, the two women ahead and the two men following. Then they went down to the river’s edge to examine an unusual water plant more closely. When they returned to the path, their positions changed slightly. Mrs. Gardiner brought about the change: tired by the morning’s exercise, she found Elizabeth’s arm did not give her enough support, and chose to take her husband’s instead.

My God! If I had imagined, even for a moment, the monstrous purpose my enemy might have in mind, I would have chosen permanent exile from my homeland, wandering the earth friendless and rejected, rather than agree to that disastrous marriage. Yet the monster had hidden his true intentions from me as effectively as if he possessed supernatural powers. Believing I had arranged only my own death, I was hastening the death of someone infinitely more precious to me.

As our wedding date approached, my heart sank, whether from cowardice or a sense of what was coming. I disguised my feelings with a show of cheerfulness that brought happiness and smiles to my father’s face, though it barely deceived Elizabeth’s more perceptive and constantly attentive eyes. She anticipated our marriage with quiet contentment, but past misfortunes had left her with a lingering fear: the happiness that now seemed so definite and within reach might dissolve into a dream, leaving behind only profound, permanent regret.

We made arrangements for the wedding and received visits from people offering their congratulations; everything around us appeared cheerful. As best I could, I kept the anxiety consuming me locked inside my heart. I joined in my father’s plans with apparent enthusiasm, although they might prove to be no more than scenery for the tragedy awaiting me. Through my father’s efforts, the Austrian government had returned part of Elizabeth’s inheritance. She now owned a small property on the shore of Lake Como. We agreed that directly after the wedding we would travel to Villa Lavenza and pass our first happy days beside the beautiful lake near the villa.

Meanwhile, I took every precaution to protect myself in case the monster attacked me openly. I always carried pistols and a dagger, and remained alert to any attempt to deceive me. These measures gave me greater peace of mind. Indeed, the nearer the wedding came, the more his threat began to seem unreal, unworthy of disturbing my peace. At the same time, the happiness I hoped to find in marriage felt increasingly certain. The date of the ceremony was approaching, and everyone continually spoke of the wedding as something that no unforeseen event could possibly stop.

Elizabeth appeared happy, and my calm manner did much to ease her mind. But on the day that would fulfil both my wishes and my fate, she grew sad, possessed by a sense that something terrible was about to happen. Perhaps she was also thinking of the dreadful secret I had promised to tell her the next day.

Merciful God! Had I for a single instant conceived the infernal design of my fiendish enemy, I would sooner have exiled myself for ever from the land of my birth, and roamed the world a solitary outcast, than consented to this wretched marriage. But the monster, as though endowed with powers of enchantment, had kept his actual purpose hidden from my sight; and while I believed I had provided for my own destruction alone, I hurried on the death of a victim far more dearly loved.

With the approach of the day appointed for our marriage, my heart failed me, whether through timidity or some prophetic apprehension. I hid this feeling beneath a semblance of gaiety, which lit my father’s face with joy and smiles, though it scarcely misled Elizabeth’s vigilant and more discerning gaze. She awaited our union in tranquil satisfaction, mingled with a slight dread, born of earlier sorrows, that the happiness which seemed now so solid and assured might melt into an insubstantial dream, leaving nothing behind save lasting and profound regret.

The arrangements went forward, visitors offered their congratulations, and everything assumed an air of gladness. I confined, so far as I was able, the anxiety gnawing at my heart within its own recesses, and appeared to embrace my father’s schemes with earnest interest, though they might serve merely to ornament my tragedy. My father’s exertions had induced the Austrian government to restore a portion of Elizabeth’s inheritance. A little estate upon the banks of Como was hers. We determined to set out for Villa Lavenza immediately after our wedding and pass the earliest days of our felicity beside the lovely lake on whose shores it stood.

During this time I neglected no precaution for my defence, should the fiend venture upon an open assault. Pistols and a dagger were always about my person, and I watched continually against deception; these measures brought me a larger share of tranquillity. Indeed, as the time drew close, the menace began to seem an illusion, hardly deserving to trouble my repose. Meanwhile the joy I expected from marriage acquired an ever greater certainty as the appointed day of its celebration neared, and as I constantly heard it discussed as an event beyond the power of any accident to hinder.

Elizabeth appeared contented; my composed behaviour greatly helped to quiet her thoughts. Yet on the day destined to accomplish my desires and seal my fate, melancholy possessed her, and a foreboding of disaster filled her mind. Perhaps she remembered, too, the terrible secret I had pledged to disclose upon the morrow.
